analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain as wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently designated about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — the coastal plain area long debated for oil drilling — as federal wilderness under the Wilderness Act. Wilderness is the strictest land protection in U.S. law: no roads, no motorized equipment, and no oil and gas leasing. Once designated, it could not be undone by a future administration without a new act of Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who values the Arctic refuge's undeveloped coastal plain — wildlife habitat for caribou, polar bears, and migratory birds, and a landscape kept off-limits to industrial development forever. Future generations inherit the protection, since wilderness designation is essentially permanent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and the refuge's wildlife

how_it_helps.text: Designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (the '1002 Area' coastal plain) as a component of the National Wilderness Preservation System under the Wilderness Act.
Because wilderness designation is permanent law, the protection could not be reversed by a future administration or Congress without enacting a new law.
The bill was introduced with 27 cosponsors (26 Democrats and 1 Independent), showing substantial Senate support for permanent protection.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry, which has long sought access to the refuge's coastal plain, loses a potential drilling frontier. The federal government and the State of Alaska forgo any future royalties or revenue from energy development there.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas developers and Alaska

drawbacks.text: The designation permanently closes the coastal plain to oil and gas development, forgoing a potential domestic energy source and the federal and state revenue that leasing and production would generate.

Alaska's congressional delegation and state leaders have historically argued that developing the area would create jobs and reduce dependence on foreign oil; this bill forecloses that option by statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is stark and essentially one-way: the bill trades potential energy development, jobs, and revenue for the permanent preservation of the largest untouched wilderness on the refuge's coastal plain. For those who prize preservation, the cost is worth it; for those who prioritize energy production, it removes the area from use forever. The bill offered no compensation or middle ground — it was an all-or-nothing designation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Lieberman introduced the bill on November 7, 2007, joined by 27 cosponsors.

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; the committee never reported it out, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests that want access to the Arctic refuge's coastal plain, since the area remains legally open to future development attempts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests seeking coastal plain access

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to designate the coastal plain as wilderness and led 27 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Barack Obama, Sen. Joseph Biden, Sen. Hillary Clinton, and Sen. Barbara Boxer
26 of 49 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a majority-sized bloc of Senate support on paper.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, marked up, or reported the bill; it sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: Alaska's senators, Ted Stevens and Lisa Murkowski
against.what_they_did: Long champions of opening the refuge's coastal plain to oil drilling; they opposed wilderness designation for the area.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 sponsors (the sponsor and 27 cosponsors) were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the Senate's Republican members generally supported drilling the area instead.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would have permanently barred drilling on the 1.56-million-acre coastal plain, one of the most contested potential oil frontiers on federal land. The industry loses a drilling opportunity; the public loses nothing it currently uses and keeps the landscape undeveloped.
Permanent wilderness protects the intact landscape that guides, outfitters, and visitors to the Arctic refuge depend on, though visitation there is small and remote.
